newsitem.title: UK: British rail firms receive ultimatum from watchdog.
newsitem.headline: British rail firms receive ultimatum from watchdog.

text.p: Britain's rail watchdog began a biteback on Wednesday by ordering train and station operators to improve service standards or face a tougher enforcement regime.
John Swift, the head of the Office of the Rail Regulator, said in a statement the time was ripe for setting out "clear, fair, achievable objectives" for the private operators.
He said it would be no longer sufficient to provide the bare minimum services and called on train operators to raise standards above those cited in their contracts.

"I am giving them a clear warning today that I will not hesitate to use my enforcement powers, including modifying licenses if that proves necessary, if improvements are not made to acceptable timescales," Swift said in a statement.
But passenger pressure group Save Our Railways (SOR) gave a frosty reception to Swift's fighting prose.

"What he's trying to do is keep his job under the new Labour government by talking tough but his powers are limited," said Jonathan Bray of SOR. "There's not much that is new here and what is really needed is a new strategic rail authority with beefed up powers."

The latest watchdog warning comes just days after Swift announced a performance review for rail infrastructure group Railtrack Plc which he said had "a long way to go" to address concerns about its performance.
On Wednesday it was the turn of the 25 nationwide passenger service franchises(train operating companies) to receive their assessments.
Swift has sent a letter to all 25 franchise chiefs with a set of guiding principles on how to improve standards.
"In return for the security of funding(government subsidy)they enjoy, operators have a duty to make a positive contribution to improve services to passengers," Swift said.
"That means more than just doing the minimum necessary to comply with their franchises and licenses."
The regulator has asked for operators to ensure services provide a "seamless national network" that promotes competition and co-operation for the benefit of passengers.
He said operators should be pro-active and use contracts with Railtrack and other players as a chance to raise standards where possible.
Further demands included making rail timetables more "stable and robust" while providing "accurate and impartial" retailing of tickets.

Swift said he would be setting up more regular assessment meetings with franchise chiefs in the coming months, heralding a more hands-on regulatory framework which was the key transport objective of the new Labour government.
John Prescott, deputy prime minister and head of the transport and environment superministry, signalled his own tougher line on private rail operators last week.
Railtrack shares shunted lower last week after Prescott warned Railtrack the price of failing to improve its performance would be fines or other sanctions.
The Association of Train Operating Companies(ATOC) said on Wednesday it welcomed the challenge thrown to its members by the regulator.
"There are still challenges to be met and the industry is committed to meeting and exceeding them," said ATOC spokesman Ivor Warburton.
But SOR's Bray denounced the objectives set by the regulator as "woolly words."
